record.paper_title: A modified star formation law as a solution to open problems in galaxy evolution
record.context_brief: Cold-gas overproduction and missing baryonic physics
record.original_question: What missing baryonic physical process or corrected cooling prescription, if any, prevents semi-analytic galaxy-formation models from overproducing cold gas while preserving successful fits to stellar masses, star-formation rates, and clustering? Candidate directions include preheating gas so that it cannot cool into low-mass haloes, feedback that preferentially heats low-entropy gas in high-redshift haloes, and revised gas-cooling treatments, but the unresolved task is to identify a process that is physically plausible and works simultaneously with the other galaxy observables.

evidence.quote:
Although there are some uncertainties related to the
determination of cold gas mass function in observation
(Keres et al. 2003; Obreschkow & Rawlings 2009; Fu et al.
2010), it seems that our models with modiﬁed SF predict
drastically too much cold gas mass in galaxies.

It is not clear up to now if
this diﬃculty in modeling galaxy properties reﬂects a fun-
damental problem in our understanding of the dark matter
universe, or if it is mainly due to an insuﬃcient understand-
ing of the baryonic physics involved in galaxy formation and
evolution.

For example, perhaps SAMs miss an important in-
gredient of galaxy formation, like a mechanism that preheat s
the gas in the universe so that it cannot cool to low mass
haloes (Mo et al. 2005, but see also Crain et al. (2007)), or
a form of feedback that mainly heats low entropy gas in
high redshift haloes (McCarthy et al. 2011). Alternatively ,
it could be that cooling is over-eﬃcient in the current SAMs
for some reason.

artifact.self_contained_problem:
In semi-analytic models (SAMs) of galaxy formation, baryonic gas is tracked through a sequence of prescriptions inside dark-matter halo merger trees: pristine gas falls into a halo and is shock-heated to the virial temperature, hot gas radiatively cools onto a central disc according to a cooling function and a chosen cooling-radius prescription, cold disc gas is converted into stars at a rate determined by an adopted star-formation law, and various feedback channels (supernova, AGN, photoionization) reheat or eject gas. By tuning their free parameters, modern SAMs can simultaneously reproduce, to acceptable accuracy, (i) the observed stellar mass function and its evolution, (ii) the cosmic and galaxy-by-galaxy star-formation rate distributions, and (iii) the two-point clustering of galaxies as a function of stellar mass. However, when a star-formation law is used that matches resolved observations of nearby galaxies (e.g., a law in which the star-formation rate surface density depends on the molecular rather than total cold-gas surface density), these same models systematically predict a cold-gas (HI + H2) mass function and cold-gas-to-stellar-mass relation that lie significantly above the observed values at low and intermediate halo masses.

Problem. Identify, within the SAM framework described above, an additional or modified baryonic prescription P with the following properties:

(a) P is physically motivated, in the sense that it corresponds to a process operating in real galaxies (for example: pre-heating of intergalactic or circumgalactic gas so that it cannot cool into low-mass haloes; a feedback channel that preferentially deposits energy in low-entropy gas in high-redshift haloes; or a corrected radiative-cooling prescription that reduces cooling efficiency in the relevant regime).

(b) When P is incorporated and the remaining free parameters are re-optimized, the resulting model brings the predicted cold-gas mass function and cold-gas-to-stellar-mass relation into agreement with observational determinations across the relevant halo-mass range.

(c) The model with P incorporated continues to reproduce, at least as well as the original calibration, the observed stellar mass function, the star-formation rate distribution, and the stellar-mass-dependent two-point clustering of galaxies.

Either exhibit such a prescription P explicitly (specifying its functional form, the haloes/redshifts on which it acts, and demonstrating (b) and (c) by re-running the model), or prove that no prescription P confined to baryonic physics within the SAM framework can simultaneously satisfy (a)–(c).
artifact.status_search_result: Subsequent work has explored each of the candidate directions—preheating, low-entropy feedback, and revised cooling prescriptions (e.g., Hou et al. 2018 MNRAS 475, 543 on a new gas-cooling model; SAGE; updated cosmological zoom comparisons)—and individual SAMs have been re-tuned to better match HI/H2 observations. However, no single physically motivated prescription has been generally accepted as simultaneously resolving cold-gas overproduction while preserving fits to stellar masses, SFRs, and clustering; the issue continues to be discussed as an open calibration tension in SAM literature.

status_evidence.title: A new gas cooling model for semi-analytic galaxy formation models
status_evidence.snippet: New models treat the evolution of the hot gas density profile and gas cooling more self-consistently compared to previous models.
status_evidence.claim: Revised cooling treatments in SAMs continue to be developed as a candidate fix, indicating the question is still being addressed.

status_evidence.title: Galaxy formation in semi-analytic models and cosmological hydrodynamic zoom simulations
status_evidence.snippet: Simulations show much higher star formation efficiencies than SAMs; cold gas is consumed much more rapidly in simulations.
status_evidence.claim: Discrepancies between SAM cold-gas predictions and other approaches remain a recognized open issue.

status_evidence.title: SAGE: Semi-Analytic Galaxy Evolution
status_evidence.snippet: Calibration of modern SAMs continues to balance stellar mass, SFR, and gas observables.
status_evidence.claim: Cold-gas calibration remains an active modeling concern, not a settled problem.
